title: Can Refinishing Fix Squeaky Hardwood Floors?
meta: Refinishing alone does not fix squeaky hardwood floors, but it is the best time to fix them: bare boards, screws hidden by sanding. Wills Flooring, Lynnwood.
keywords: can refinishing fix squeaky floors, squeaky hardwood floors fix, why do hardwood floors squeak, fix squeaks before refinishing, hardwood floor refinishing Lynnwood WA

blocks.lead: No. Sanding and finishing only touch the top of the boards, and squeaks come from movement underneath: boards rubbing on loose nails, or the subfloor lifting off a joist. But a refinish is the single best time to fix squeaks, because the floor is bare, the crew is already there, and the screws and plugs disappear under the sanding and finish.
blocks.detail: We fix squeaks as part of the refinish on most Lynnwood jobs. A natural sand and refinish is $3.99 per sq ft, and squeak repair is scoped at the free estimate once we have walked the floor and, where possible, looked at it from the crawlspace.

blocks.html: This one comes up constantly in Lynnwood, because so many Alderwood and Martha Lake ramblers from the 1960s and 70s have original oak under the carpet, and the moment the carpet comes up the squeaks the pad was muffling are suddenly loud. Owners assume a refinish will make the floor new in every sense. It will make it look new. It will not make it quiet unless the crew deals with the movement first.

blocks.text: Why hardwood floors squeak in the first place

items.title: Boards moving on their nails
items.text: Old cut nails and 1970s cleats lose grip as the wood dries out over 50 winters. The board lifts a hair when you step off it and rides back down the nail shank with a chirp. This is the most common Lynnwood squeak and the easiest to fix during a refinish.

items.title: Subfloor lifting off the joists
items.text: Plank or plywood subfloor that was nailed, not glued and screwed, pulls away from the joist over time. The whole area creaks rather than chirps. It is fixed from below through the crawlspace or from above with screws into the joist.

items.title: Seasonal shrinkage
items.text: Boards shrink in the dry heat of a Lynnwood winter and rub against each other at the tongue and groove. These squeaks come and go with the season. Finish does not touch them, but stable humidity in the house does.

items.title: Something else entirely
items.text: Ductwork rubbing a joist, a loose bridging block, a pipe strapped too tight. If the squeak is under the floor rather than in it, we tell you at the estimate instead of charging for a fix that would not work.

blocks.text: What a refinish does and does not do to a squeak

a.title: What it changes
items: Removes the old finish, scratches and gray boards
Fills small gaps and nail holes with matching filler
Locks the surface fibers with three coats of Bona water-based finish
Can slightly stiffen a loose top edge with filler, but only cosmetically

b.title: What it leaves alone
items: The nails and cleats that have lost their grip
The gap between subfloor and joist
Boards rubbing each other at the tongue
Any noise coming from ducts, pipes or blocking below

blocks.text: Why Lynnwood floors squeak more than most

items.text: Alderwood, Meadowdale and Martha Lake homes have 1x6 or 1x8 plank subfloors laid diagonally and nailed to the joists. Fifty years of drying shrinks those planks and loosens the nails under the oak. The crawlspace usually lets us fix it from below.

The upper level sits over a garage or family room with no crawlspace access. Squeaks there are fixed from above with screws through the hardwood, which is exactly why doing it during a refinish, when the holes get sanded and filled, is so much cleaner.

items.d: Oak that spent decades under carpet
items.text: Carpet and pad hide squeaks and hold moisture against the wood. When the carpet comes up, expect the floor to sound worse for a week as it dries, then settle. We walk it after that.

Most Lynnwood ramblers run forced air with no humidification. Winter indoor humidity drops into the 20s, boards shrink, and tongue-and-groove squeaks show up in January and vanish in June. A humidifier is cheaper than any floor repair.

blocks.text: When a squeak means you should not refinish yet

items.html: The floor is bouncy, not just noisy. Deflection means a joist or subfloor problem. Screws through the hardwood will not fix it, and sanding a floor that will be opened up later is wasted money.
There is a soft spot near a bathroom or the back door. That is usually rot from a slow leak. The boards and sometimes the subfloor need replacing before any finish goes on.

The boards are too thin for another sanding. Oak that has been sanded three or four times may have less than 3/32 inch above the tongue. Driving screws through it can split it. We measure at the estimate and will say so if a screen and recoat is the smarter move.
The squeak is under a floating floor. If engineered plank is floating over the noise, refinishing is not even the right category of fix.

blocks.title: Do not let anyone talk you into this:
blocks.text: Face-nailing squeaky boards with finish nails and calling it done. The nails lose grip within a year and now you have a squeak plus a row of holes. Screws hold; nails do not.
How to get a quiet floor out of your refinish

items: Walk the floor with the estimator and mark every squeak with painter's tape before the quote is written.
Ask whether the crew fixes squeaks from above, from below, or both, and how the screw holes are hidden.
Clear the crawlspace hatch if your Lynnwood rambler has one.
Expect the floor to sound worse for the first week after carpet removal; the real walk-test is after that.
Keep the house between 35 and 55 percent humidity after the finish cures.
Get squeak repair as a written line item, separate from the $3.99 per sq ft refinish rate, and confirm the 1-year workmanship warranty covers it.

faq.q: Will sanding and refinishing make my hardwood floors stop squeaking?
faq.a: Not on its own. Sanding removes finish and a thin layer of wood from the top; squeaks come from boards or subfloor moving on loose fasteners underneath. A refinish is the ideal time to fix squeaks, because screws driven through the bare boards get filled and sanded invisible, but it has to be done deliberately.

faq.q: How do you fix a squeaky floor without leaving visible holes?
faq.a: Trim-head screws are driven at an angle through the board into the subfloor or joist, sunk just below the surface. The hole is filled with matching wood filler during the refinish, then sanded flush and finished over. On a natural or medium-toned floor the repair is nearly impossible to find afterward.

faq.q: Can squeaks be fixed from the crawlspace instead?
faq.a: Yes, and it is our first choice when a Lynnwood rambler has crawlspace access. A shim with construction adhesive closes the gap between joist and subfloor, and screws up through the subfloor pull the hardwood tight. Nothing touches the finished surface, so it can be done before or after refinishing.

faq.q: How much does squeak repair add to a refinish?
faq.a: It depends on how many areas need screws and whether we work from above or below. It is quoted per area at the free estimate after we walk the floor with you. The refinish itself stays at the published rate, $3.99 per sq ft for natural and $6.50 with stain, with a 500 sq ft minimum.

faq.q: Why did my floor start squeaking after the carpet was removed?
faq.a: It was probably squeaking all along, and the carpet and pad were muffling it. Carpet also holds moisture against the oak, so the boards dry and shrink for a week or two after removal, which loosens nails further. We walk-test after that settling period.

faq.q: Do squeaks mean the floor is unsafe or rotten?
faq.a: Usually not. A chirp from a single board is loose nails, not damage. What we take seriously is bounce, a soft spot, or a squeak near a bathroom or exterior door, since those can mean subfloor rot or a joist issue. We check for all three at the estimate before recommending a refinish.
